title: Indian Graduates Who Go Home See Their Income Multiply 8.4 Times. A New Report Explains Why.
excerpt: India hit a record $135 billion in remittances last year. A 12-year study of 25,000 students shows exactly where that money comes from — and what happens when it flows the other way.
body:
A new report from MPOWER Financing puts hard numbers behind a story that every Indian family with a child abroad already knows intuitively: studying overseas transforms earnings, and the returns flow in both directions.

The 2026 Social Impact Report, released on June 8, draws on twelve years of data covering more than 25,000 students from 183 countries. The headline finding for India: graduates who return home after studying abroad see their income grow 8.4 times compared to their pre-departure earnings. The country-level picture is equally striking — India recorded a record $135 billion in remittances in FY2025, a 14 percent year-on-year increase, partly fuelled by the earning power of its international graduates.

## The Largest Pipeline in the World

India remains the single largest source of international graduate students in the United States, with enrollment rising 19 percent to nearly 200,000. The majority are pursuing postgraduate degrees in engineering, data science, business, and healthcare — fields that align directly with North America's most acute skills shortages.

MPOWER, which provides no-cosigner education loans to international students, says its Indian borrowers represent a particularly high-ambition, career-driven segment. The company has now funded over $1 billion in tuition across its twelve-year history.

The report puts human faces on the macro data. Seventy-seven percent of MPOWER graduates who are employed full-time send money home, averaging $6,000 annually. For families earning $15,000 or less per year — a bracket that includes a significant share of households in tier-two and tier-three Indian cities — that single contribution represents a 40 to 50 percent increase in total household income.

## The Financing Bottleneck

Perhaps the most telling data point in the report: 93 percent of MPOWER's global borrower base said they would not have been able to study abroad without the company's support. For Indian students specifically, the constraint is structural. Traditional lenders require collateral or US-based cosigners — barriers that effectively lock out talented students from middle-class families without property assets or American relatives.

The finding underscores a persistent gap in India's education-to-emigration pipeline. The demand is enormous, the returns are proven, and the macroeconomic benefits to India — through remittances, skills transfer, and diaspora networks — are well documented. But the financing infrastructure remains thin, leaving families to mortgage homes or borrow at high interest from informal lenders.

MPOWER's model, which underwrites students based on future earning potential rather than current collateral, has been gaining traction precisely because of this gap. The company's data suggests that betting on Indian students' career trajectories has been, by the numbers, a sound financial proposition.

## The Return Premium

The 8.4x income multiplier for returning graduates challenges a persistent assumption in Indian diaspora conversations: that staying abroad is always the better financial move. While US salaries in technology and healthcare remain substantially higher in absolute terms, the purchasing power parity gap, combined with India's lower cost of living and rapidly growing private sector, means that return migrants can command salaries that place them firmly in India's upper-middle class.

The dynamic is particularly relevant in 2026, as the US job market faces uncertainty from AI-driven restructuring and renewed rate-hike concerns. The H-1B pathway, long the default for Indian graduates, is also becoming more selective under proposed salary-weighted selection rules. For some graduates, returning home may not just be a lifestyle choice — it may be the pragmatic one.

## What the Numbers Mean for NRIs

For established NRIs, the report offers both validation and a subtle prompt. The $135 billion remittance figure — which has nearly doubled from $70 billion a decade ago — confirms that the diaspora's economic connection to India is intensifying, not fading. But it also highlights how much of that connection depends on the continued flow of students abroad.

Any disruption to that pipeline — tighter visa rules, higher tuition, less accessible financing — would be felt not just by individual families but in India's current account, its housing markets, and the growing ecosystem of NRI-linked investment that sustains everything from real estate in Hyderabad to gold demand during Diwali.

The MPOWER data makes the case that investing in Indian students abroad is not charity. It is, by every measure, one of the highest-returning investments either country can make.
